passages.happening:
“This is the blessing that Moses the man of God pronounced upon the Israelites before his death” (verse 1).

It does not begin with the tribes. It begins with God. “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned upon us from Seir; He shone forth from Mount Paran and came with myriads of holy ones” (verse 2).

Moses turns and speaks to God: ‘Surely You love the people; all the holy ones are in Your hand, and they sit down at Your feet’ (verse 3). The people received the law that Moses gave, ‘the possession of the assembly of Jacob’ (verse 4). “So the LORD became King in Jeshurun when the leaders of the people gathered, when the tribes of Israel came together” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The song of chapter 32 was a warning. This is the other thing Moses leaves behind him. His last words to Israel are words of blessing.

In the ancient world a father's blessing before his death was a weighty thing. It was more than a kind wish. It was believed to shape what came after. Genesis ends with Jacob blessing his twelve sons, and Deuteronomy ends with Moses blessing the twelve tribes that came from them. Moses is called here ‘the man of God’, a title used for prophets. He blesses Israel as a father would.

The opening picture is of a sunrise. God ‘dawned’ and ‘shone forth’. God is pictured as a king coming with his attendants to meet his people.

Three things are said about that meeting, and they belong together. God loves the people. The people sit at his feet and receive his words. And he becomes their king. In this book the law is the gift of a king who loves. It is called Israel's ‘possession’, its inheritance, the thing handed down.

Jeshurun is the poetic name for Israel used in the song, where it was spoken with bitter irony. Here it is used with honor. God still calls his people by what he means them to be.
passages.later:
Genesis ends as this book ends, with a blessing on each tribe: “He blessed them, and he blessed each one with a suitable blessing” (Genesis 49:28).

One psalm carries Moses' name, and its title uses the words of verse 1: ‘A prayer of Moses the man of God’ (Psalm 90:1).

A psalm sums up what this passage says of Israel: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people He has chosen as His inheritance!” (Psalm 33:12).
passages.asks: Moses' last words to a people he knew would fail were a blessing. Ask what your last words to the people you love would be, and whether they hear anything like it from you now. And notice that the law is called a possession. Ask whether you receive God's word as an inheritance or as a weight.

passages.happening:
Moses blesses the tribes one by one.

For Reuben: ‘Let Reuben live and not die’ (verse 6). For Judah, a prayer that God will hear his cry and be ‘a help against his foes’ (verse 7).

For Levi, the longest after Joseph's. Levi kept God's word even against his own family. “He will teach Your ordinances to Jacob and Your law to Israel; he will set incense before You and whole burnt offerings on Your altar” (verse 10).

For Benjamin: “May the beloved of the LORD rest secure in Him; God shields him all day long, and upon His shoulders he rests” (verse 12).

For Joseph, a long blessing of dew, deep waters, sun and harvest, ‘and with the favor of Him who dwelt in the burning bush’ (verse 16).

Then Zebulun and Issachar, Gad, Dan and Naphtali, each with a line or two (verses 18-23). And for Asher: ‘may your strength match your days’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The sayings differ greatly in length. Reuben has one line. Joseph has five verses. Several use pictures of animals, a lion, a lion's cub and a wild ox, as Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49 does.

Levi's blessing looks back to the golden calf. When Moses called for those on the LORD's side, the Levites came to him and stood for God even against their own relatives. Their work is given in verse 10, and teaching comes first. The priest in Israel was a teacher of God's law before he was anything else. The Urim and Thummim of verse 8 were objects kept by the high priest and used to seek God's decision in hard matters. How they worked is not known.

Benjamin's blessing is one of the gentlest in the Bible. The picture is of someone carried and kept safe.

Joseph stands for two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh. His blessing dwells on the richness of the land, because in a country that lived by rain, a good harvest was a direct gift of God. It also names God as the one ‘who dwelt in the burning bush’. Moses, at the end of his life, remembers where it began.

Simeon is not named. In the book of Joshua that tribe's land lies inside Judah's, and it seems to have been absorbed into Judah early. That may be why.

Some of the sayings seem to describe the tribes as already settled in the land. Readers who hold that Moses wrote the blessing take them as spoken beforehand. Others think they reflect the tribes' later circumstances. These notes do not settle it.

Verse 11 and verse 17 use the hard language of battle. They are part of an ancient blessing on tribes about to enter a contested land. They are not a pattern for anyone's conduct now.
passages.later:
Jacob's blessing gave Judah the place that Moses' short prayer does not spell out: “The scepter will not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:10). King David came from that tribe, and the letter to the Hebrews notes that ‘our Lord descended from Judah’ (Hebrews 7:14).

Exodus tells what lies behind Levi's blessing: “Whoever is for the LORD, come to me.” ‘And all the Levites gathered around him’ (Exodus 32:26).

The prophet Malachi held the priests of his day to the charge of verse 10: “For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth” (Malachi 2:7).
passages.asks: Each tribe received a different word, and none was left out except by a silence the text does not explain. Ask what particular gift and task you have been given, and whether you envy another's. And take the last line as your own prayer: ask for strength to match your days, however many they are.

passages.happening:
The blessing ends as it began, with God.

“There is none like the God of Jeshurun, who rides the heavens to your aid, and the clouds in His majesty” (verse 26).

“The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (verse 27). He drives out the enemy before Israel. “So Israel dwells securely”, in a land of grain and new wine, where the heavens drip with dew (verse 28).

And the last words Moses speaks in the book: “Blessed are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD? He is the shield that protects you” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The blessings on the tribes are held between two hymns, one at the start and one here. Whatever each tribe receives, it receives from this God.

Two pictures of God are set side by side in verses 26 and 27. In the first he is above, riding the heavens and coming to help. In the second he is beneath. ‘Underneath are the everlasting arms.’ However far a person falls, there is something lower still, and it holds.

The word translated ‘dwelling place’ can mean a refuge or a den, the place an animal goes to be safe. Israel is about to enter a land and build houses. Moses says that its real home is God himself. The one psalm that bears Moses' name opens with nearly the same word.

Think of who is saying this. Moses has no home in the land. He will die within sight of it, on the wrong side of the river. A man in that position says that the eternal God is a dwelling place, and that underneath are the everlasting arms. He is speaking of what he knows.

The last sentence calls Israel ‘a people saved by the LORD’. The Hebrew word for ‘saved’ is the root of the names Joshua and Jesus. Here it means rescue from enemies, the kind of rescue Israel had known since the exodus.

Verse 27 and verse 29 speak of enemies driven out and trodden down. They belong with the commands of chapter 7. The note on chapter 7, verses 1 to 5, sets out how Christians read them, and says that no one may use them to justify violence.

‘Who is like you?’ is not a boast about Israel. The reason given is not anything in Israel. It is that the LORD saved them. The book has said from the start that Israel was chosen out of love and not for its size or its goodness.
passages.later:
The psalm of Moses begins where his blessing ends: “Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations” (Psalm 90:1).

Isaiah heard God promise to carry his people to the end of their lives: “Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray” (Isaiah 46:4).

Paul gives the Christian form of the same confidence: nothing in all creation ‘will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord’ (Romans 8:39).
passages.asks: Moses said this with no home of his own to go to. Ask where you look for a place to be safe, and whether it can bear your weight. Then take verse 27 slowly. Ask whether you believe that beneath the lowest point you can reach, the arms of God are still under you.
